find: On BAILII (bailii.org) under United Kingdom House of Lords Decisions, free and complete. The Appeal Cases citation will find it in any library carrying the English reports. Read the majority speeches rather than a summary; the reasoning is why this case is read and the outcome is not.
why: The case the whole of negligence grew out of, and the source of the neighbour principle your lesson states. It belongs first in this module because everything else here — Caparo's caution about single grand tests most of all — is a reaction to it.

read.passage: The passage stating the neighbour principle.
read.look_for: Write it in your own words before reading on. Then ask what it requires: who counts as a neighbour, and by what test. The phrase is famous and the test inside it is what does the work.

read.passage: The reasoning about why the absence of a contract was not fatal.
read.look_for: Follow the move from contract to a duty owed independently of it. That move is the reason tort could develop at all, and it is easy to miss because it now seems obvious.

read.passage: Any dissent, and what it warns about.
read.look_for: The dissent is not foolish. Ask what it feared would follow from a general principle — then read Caparo and notice who was proved partly right.

questions.q: State the neighbour principle in one sentence and say what makes someone a neighbour.
questions.model: A good answer gives both halves. The principle is easy to half-remember as a duty to avoid harming others, which is too wide to be a legal test. The useful part is the limiting idea inside it — closeness and foreseeability of harm to this claimant — and an answer without a limiting idea has quoted a slogan.

questions.q: Read this alongside Caparo. What is Caparo reacting to?
questions.model: A good answer sees that Caparo's incremental method is a response to the risk of reasoning from one broad principle: a general test lets a court find a duty in a situation nobody has considered, with no comparison case to discipline it. Reading them in this order shows the argument as a development rather than two unrelated tests.

questions.q: This is a 1932 Scottish appeal to the House of Lords. What is its standing in Malaysia?
questions.model: A good answer places it under section 3 of the Civil Law Act 1956: it predates the reception dates, so it comes in as part of the received common law so far as local circumstances permit. That is a stronger position than the post-reception English cases in this module, and saying why is the point.

trap: Treating the neighbour principle as the modern test for duty. It is where the modern law starts, and the module's later cases are the corrections; an answer that stops here is sixty years short.
source: Citation taken from the glossary entry for the term "neighbour" in this corpus, which states it in full.
verify: Check the citation on BAILII. Confirm how the Malaysian courts state the current duty test before relying on the neighbour principle as the operative rule.

case: Associated Provincial Picture Houses Ltd v Wednesbury Corporation
find: On BAILII (bailii.org) under England and Wales Court of Appeal decisions, free. The King's Bench citation will find it in a library. It is short, and the passage everyone cites is shorter still — read the surrounding reasoning as well as the famous sentence.
why: The source of a word your lesson uses as a ground of review. Read it to find out how narrow the original formulation is, and how much of what people call Wednesbury unreasonableness the case itself never said.

read.passage: The passage describing a decision so unreasonable that no reasonable authority could have made it.
read.look_for: Note how high that sets the bar. Then ask how often a real decision could clear it, and what that implies about how often this ground succeeds.

read.passage: The court's list of the other things that can vitiate a decision.
read.look_for: The famous ground is one item among several. The others — irrelevant considerations, improper purpose — are separately arguable, and are the ones that usually do the work.

read.passage: Anything about the court's own role relative to the authority's.
read.look_for: This is the constitutional point underneath the test: why a court reviews the decision-making rather than the decision. It is the same distinction your lesson draws.

questions.q: State the unreasonableness ground as this case actually puts it, and say how demanding it is.
questions.model: A good answer reproduces the structure rather than the phrase — a decision no reasonable authority could have reached — and then says plainly that the bar is very high and the ground rarely succeeds alone. An answer that treats it as meaning simply unreasonable has adopted the loose usage the case does not support.

questions.q: Why is it a mistake to run this ground on its own?
questions.model: A good answer notes that the same judgment names other, more tractable failings — irrelevant considerations, improper purpose — and that most successful challenges run those. Naming the ground that fits the facts, rather than the ground with the famous name, is the practical skill.

questions.q: Your glossary says this was received in Malaysia. What should you check before relying on that?
questions.model: A good answer treats reception as a claim to verify rather than a licence: check the Malaysian authorities on the grounds of review, and whether an apex court here has restated or extended them. The glossary is a study aid, not authority, and this course's own rule is to go to the source.

trap: Using the word as a synonym for wrong. It names a specific and very demanding ground, and using it loosely in a submission signals that you have not read the case it comes from.
source: Citation taken from the glossary entry for "Wednesbury unreasonableness" in this corpus, which states it in full and notes it as received in Malaysia.
verify: Check the citation on BAILII, and check how the Malaysian courts currently state the grounds of judicial review before treating this formulation as the local test.

case: QSR Brands Bhd v Suruhanjaya Sekuriti
find: Malaysian Court of Appeal decisions of this period are on CommonLII (commonlii.org, Malaysia) and through the government Court Case Judgment Search at malaysia.gov.my. The MLJ citation will find it in a law library.
why: A Malaysian appellate court on the Order 53 procedure your lesson and the statute tier both rest on. Read it with Order 53 open — the case is about how the rule works, and the rule is short enough to have in front of you.

read.passage: The court's treatment of the leave requirement and what it is for.
read.look_for: Ask what leave is filtering out. A threshold exists to stop something; naming what it stops tells you how hard it should be to cross.

read.passage: Anything about who may apply, and the interest they must show.
read.look_for: Standing is where many applications die. Note precisely what has to be shown and by whom.

read.passage: Passages dealing with the relationship between the procedure and the substantive grounds.
read.look_for: Procedure and grounds are separate questions that get argued together. Watch where the court keeps them apart.

questions.q: What does the leave stage decide, and what does it not decide?
questions.model: A good answer distinguishes the threshold from the merits: leave asks whether there is an arguable case fit for further consideration, not whether the applicant should win. Collapsing the two is the commonest error, and it produces submissions that argue the whole case at the wrong hearing.

questions.q: Read this with Order 53 in the statute tier. What does the case add to the rule?
questions.model: A good answer identifies something the rule's words leave open and the court settles — how a requirement is applied, or what an expression covers. That is what case law adds to a procedural rule, and an answer that merely restates the rule has not used the case.

trap: Treating judicial review as a single question. Leave, standing, grounds and remedy are four separate hurdles, and an application can be perfectly arguable on the grounds and still fail at the first.
source: Citation taken from the glossary entry for "Order 53" in this corpus, which states it in full.
verify: Check the citation and the court against the report, and read the current Order 53 alongside it — the Rules of Court have been amended and the procedure may not be as this case found it.

find: A Malayan Law Journal citation from 1967; law libraries carrying the MLJ series will have it, and many Malaysian university libraries admit visitors. CommonLII's Malaysian coverage for this period is thin, so the printed report is likely the reliable route.
why: A case about which earlier decisions bind a Malaysian court, from the period when that question was genuinely open. Read it for how a court reasons about its own place in a hierarchy — which is the skill the sources lesson is building.

read.passage: The court's account of which decisions it considers itself bound by, and why.
read.look_for: Follow the reasoning about authority rather than the outcome. The question is where binding force comes from, and courts rarely have to say so explicitly.

read.passage: Anything about decisions of courts that no longer stand above this one.
read.look_for: Hierarchies change. Ask what happens to the authority of a decision when the court that made it is no longer superior — the answer is not obvious and it is the reason this case is cited.

questions.q: What makes a decision binding on a Malaysian court — the court that made it, or the court's position when it made it?
questions.model: A good answer sees that the question has two possible answers and that the case is where the difference matters. It should say which the court adopted and what follows for decisions made before a change in the hierarchy. An answer that assumes the modern position without noticing it was ever open has missed why the case is read.

questions.q: Why does a problem about precedent in Malaysia need history that an English one does not?
questions.model: A good answer connects to the corpus: the court structure changed, appeals to an external final court were abolished, and the authority of decisions from that era has to be worked out rather than assumed. The relevant statute is the Courts of Judicature Act 1964, which the problem this case comes from also cites.

trap: Reading it as settling the modern position. It is a decision from a period when the hierarchy was different, and its value is the reasoning about authority rather than a rule you can transplant.
